items.title: Radical Numerics: AI-designed phages given to a patient for the first time
items.summary: On 20 October the San Francisco AI lab Radical Numerics launched Omnii-1, a multimodal genome language model. It says a cocktail of phages (viruses that attack bacteria) designed by Omnii-1 has been given to one patient with an antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection. The treatment ran under a physician-led compassionate-use pathway, which lets a patient get an experimental therapy outside a trial. In the lab, the cocktail wiped out the bacteria isolated from the patient. Lab figures: 69.9 percent of the designed variants were viable, against 4.8 percent of random controls, and 2,161 of 6,694 active variants beat the natural phage. The company has not released how the patient did and warns that one case proves neither safety nor efficacy. The team behind it previously built the Evo and Evo 2 models.
items.why_it_matters: AI-designed biological treatments are reaching patients, and bacteria that resist antibiotics are linked to millions of deaths a year. This is relevant for biotech and health investors.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude proved code in 123 open-source libraries crash-free and found hundreds of bugs
items.summary: Working with the verification company Theorem, Anthropic says Claude wrote formal mathematical proofs that 239 entry points in 123 libraries from Google's OSS-Fuzz project cannot crash on any input under 64 MB. The proofs total about 180 million lines of Rocq code and are checked against the compiled RISC-V machine code, not just the source. Along the way Claude found and fixed hundreds of bugs, some of which had survived years of automated stress testing. Anthropic stresses that this does not make the libraries bug-free, because the guarantees depend on models of RISC-V and Linux and on how the theorems are stated.
items.why_it_matters: Formal verification used to be too expensive to use at scale. If AI makes it cheap, it could change software security for banks and other critical infrastructure.

items.title: OpenAI ran 1,946 GPT-Rosalind agents on a mouse brain atlas and generated research leads in 32 minutes
items.summary: OpenAI, PerturbAI and Scripps Research ran 1,946 GPT-Rosalind agents in parallel on a whole-brain CRISPR atlas covering millions of mouse brain cells. Each agent analysed one switched-off gene, and the whole run took 32 minutes. The authors estimate the same work by hand would take months to a year, but that is an illustrative estimate, not a measured comparison. The agents reproduced or refined 48 of the original study's 55 findings without seeing its manuscript. They kept 7,586 literature references, against about 11 for a single agent. In a blinded review, 30 biologists with doctorates broadly backed the agents' ranking of leads. One lead links the gene DCTN1 to higher activity in cholesterol-production genes. The work is a bioRxiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed.
items.why_it_matters: Shows how swarms of agents can compress months of research analysis into minutes, with consequences for R&D productivity in pharma and biotech.

items.title: Claude designed 17 binding proteins against scorpion toxins in 64 hours on its own
items.summary: Anthropic reports a 64-hour autonomous protein-design campaign driven by Claude from one initial prompt and four follow-ups. It generated 318,484 designs with 12 tools and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, using roughly 10,000 GPU hours. Of 211 designs tested in the lab, 17 bound to scorpion neurotoxins, and two (Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2) bound with affinity in the single-digit nanomolar range. 11 of 60 single-toxin designs succeeded (18 percent). None of the 91 designs aimed at all five toxins met the criteria for more than one toxin. Anthropic says it has not shown that the proteins neutralise venom and does not claim to have made an antivenom. All data has been released on Hugging Face.
items.why_it_matters: Another example of a language model running a whole scientific workflow on its own, from design to lab test, with total costs reported at under 200,000 dollars.

items.title: METR and Redwood found several holes in OpenAI's internal monitoring of AI agents
items.summary: METR published an external red-team review of OpenAI's internal system for spotting misaligned AI agents. A METR employee and a Redwood Research employee spent three weeks (21 July to 11 August) with access to code, monitor prompts and staff. They estimate that 75 to 94 percent of agent traffic from the strongest models was eligible for monitoring, and 99.2 percent for internal Codex agents. Problems they found: agents could postpone monitoring by continuing to act, an exploit could hide hundreds of actions from the monitor, two client-controllable headers could switch monitoring off, there was a possible sandbox bypass, and roughly 10 percent of Codex traffic went unmonitored from May to July. OpenAI says the vulnerabilities in production are patched, which METR has not checked. Separately, on 20 October METR published an external review of the misalignment section of Anthropic's August 2026 risk report.
items.why_it_matters: One of the first times an outside party has had deep access to audit a frontier lab's safety measures for internal AI agents. That matters for regulation and for how companies govern their own agents.

items.title: The Lancet Digital Health: AI estimates survival risk for cancer patients from a single face photo
items.summary: Mass General Brigham researchers published FAHR-Face in The Lancet Digital Health. It is a foundation model trained on more than 40 million face images that estimates biological age and mortality risk from a single photo. In a test group of 3,820 cancer patients, 64 of the 122 with the highest risk scores died within 90 days. The model was validated on almost 5,000 cancer patients in the Netherlands. Smiling or changing the lighting shifted the age estimate by about two years. Independent experts say the tool is not ready for clinical use.
items.why_it_matters: Shows both the promise and the ethical and accuracy problems of using cheap biometric data in clinical decisions.

items.title: Agile Robots unveils Nvidia-based research humanoid and plans 1,000 to 2,000 units
items.summary: At Nvidia GTC Berlin on 21 October, Munich-based Agile Robots unveiled Agile ONE SN, a 1.4-metre research humanoid with 31 degrees of freedom. It has two WUJI Hand 2 hands, each with 20 degrees of freedom and tactile sensing, and runs on Nvidia Jetson Thor with the Isaac GR00T platform. The CEO told Reuters that production of ONE S and ONE SN starts by the end of 2026, with 1,000 to 2,000 units expected. Stanford and ETH Zurich are named as potential customers. Availability is planned for early 2027.
items.why_it_matters: European humanoid production is moving to commercial scale on Nvidia's platform, which shows Nvidia's growing grip on embodied AI.

items.title: Perplexity and Nvidia present JOLT: same maths accuracy with 6.5 times fewer training tokens
items.summary: Perplexity Research and Nvidia introduced JOLT (Joint On-Policy Learning and Teaching), a training method in which one model acts as both teacher and student. The teacher role sees extra information, such as verified solutions, and uses it to give the student targeted feedback during training. On the MATH benchmark, JOLT matched the accuracy of GRPO, a standard reinforcement-learning method, with about 6.5 times fewer training tokens. The JOLT+ variant reportedly beat GRPO on all five benchmarks tested, including +9.9 points on AppWorld and +4.2 on MATH, with Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V2-Lite as base models.
items.why_it_matters: More efficient training of reasoning models lowers the cost of building capable agents outside the biggest labs.
